extracted.intended_audience: speculative-fiction writers and worldbuilders concerned with cultural appropriation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writers on how to avoid cultural appropriation when creating fictional cultures and settings, with alternatives, research practices, and examples from film. Focuses on ethical, representational, and practical criteria for worldbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid caricature, demonization, trivialization, and inaccuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural appropriation in worldbuilding occurs when the depiction of a culture is caricatured, demonized, trivialized, or simply inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any effort by the storyteller to make the culture 'cool, entertaining, exotic, or mysterious' will not be received well. Treat cultural depiction with nuance; avoid turning real-world groups into one-note or sensationalized elements. Example framing: if a depiction reads like a caricature or is blatantly incorrect, it's likely appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't mix-and-match unrelated cultures (avoid cultural blenderism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldbuilders often put multiple cultures in a blender instead of depicting a specific culture authentically, which can erase the identities those cultures belong to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing elements from many cultures into a single fictional culture creates incoherent and appropriative stand-ins. If you draw from multiple sources, be deliberate about which aspects you adapt and why — and avoid implying the combined result 'represents' any real group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generalizing or lumping whole regions/continents together
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldbuilders often lump other cultures together (for example, using one culture to represent all of East Asia or the continent of Africa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present a fictional culture as a generic proxy for a vast, diverse set of peoples. Treat cultures as internally diverse; specificity matters. Lumping flattens differences and perpetuates stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on cultural stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Including a culture because you want a trope (e.g., 'nature-loving tribes' or 'fortune-telling Roma stand-ins') is stereotyping, which is appropriative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using real-world cultural groups as shorthand for traits or plot devices. Instead develop characters, institutions, and beliefs internally consistent to your world rather than borrowing stock stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calling a culture by another name doesn't erase the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling a culture by another name does not get rid of appropriation; fictional cultures that function as stand-ins for real ones can still be appropriative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renaming or relabeling a depiction (changing labels, place names, or ethnic markers) is not sufficient if the depiction is recognizably derived from or standing in for a real culture without authentic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer alternatives to directly using another culture as your setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the difficulty of authentic depiction, it's often better not to use another culture for a whole setting; alternatives exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include: make your culture unique enough that it isn't a stand-in for a real one; base your culture on powerful Western imperial cultures (if you must reuse familiar systems); depict your own culture or a fictional stand-in for it; or choose a very specific culture and study it deeply. The author recommends avoiding wholesale adoption of another culture unless you can do it responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: If depicting a specific real culture, commit to deep study and hire consultants
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a very specific culture and fully dedicate yourself to studying that culture in depth. Hire consultants of that culture and prioritize representing it authentically over anything else in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include parts of the culture that its people don't want depicted. Authenticity requires prioritizing the culture's perspectives, hiring people from that culture (consultants, actors, designers), and adjusting story/production choices based on their input. Case studies: Black Panther used Black writers/directors and designers; Moana used consultants but still produced a mishmash when leadership lacked lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether you have the resources and responsibility to depict a whole culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Most storytellers lack the budget and dedication necessary to depict an entire culture authentically; writing a novel is less likely to provide jobs to many people of a depicted culture and more likely to compete with stories written by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don't have the resources for thorough research, community engagement, and meaningful inclusion, reconsider using another culture as a setting. Support diversity in storytellers instead of expecting privileged creators to tell non-Western settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the 'why' behind cultural practices rather than copying specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: When doing worldbuilding research, focus on the why of the culture (e.g., environmental and economic reasons) instead of copying specific artifacts, foods, or ritual details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ecological/functional reasoning (e.g., what flora/fauna exist in a region and how that shapes diet, burial practices, etc.) to invent culturally plausible elements rather than transplanting real-world dishes, names, or sacred items. Example: understand why the Inuit get most of their calories from animals, then design analogous practices for your fictional northern culture without using Inuit-specific foods or terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cross-cultural comparison as inspiration but package elements appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Many specific behaviors are repeated across multiple cultures and are fair game so long as you package them appropriately and avoid direct appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study how different cultures handle the same problem (e.g., disposal of the dead) to generate ideas. If multiple cultures share a practice (e.g., ritual ingestion of mind-altering substances), you may adapt the idea, but avoid using labels, names, or symbols tied to a particular culture (e.g., calling something 'Spirit Quest' ties it to Native Americans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exploiting cultural artifacts or attempting to claim ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not commercialize or legally appropriate culturally significant terms or practices (e.g., attempting to trademark a holiday name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect cultural ownership and communal meaning—efforts like attempting to trademark Día de los Muertos are examples of cultural theft. Be cautious about profiting from or legally claiming exclusive rights over cultural items or terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and defer to creators from underrepresented groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Under-represented groups deserve to benefit from their own settings; support greater diversity in storytellers rather than centering privileged creators in non-Western stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, amplify and create opportunities for writers from the cultures you wish to depict. Recognize the market/economic harm appropriation can do—privileged storytellers can push marginalized creators out of opportunities.
